expert_diagnosis: The Maytas acquisition proposal was a visible manifestation of a deep governance and financial fraud. The promoter's attempt to transfer company cash (which was later revealed to be falsified/non-existent) into personal real-estate assets through related-party acquisitions was a classic fraud-concealment maneuver. Root causes: governance failure, related-party transaction risk, financial-statement reliability risk, board oversight failure, fraud risk, capital allocation red flag, and promoter-control risk.
expert_first_action: Halt related-party acquisition immediately (done); commission independent forensic audit of all bank balances and cash positions; replace or strengthen independent directors immediately; engage SEBI and auditors for emergency review; do not proceed with any corporate actions until financial truth is independently verified; protect customers and employees from disruption during investigation.
actual_decision: Acquisition withdrawn under investor pressure on 16 December 2008. No forensic audit or independent verification was immediately commissioned. Ramalinga Raju confessed on 7 January 2009.
harmful_actions: Board approved related-party acquisition without independent scrutiny
No independent forensic audit commissioned after investor alarm
Promoter maintained control after governance red flag was identified
Auditors (PricewaterhouseCoopers) failed to detect falsified accounts
beneficial_actions: Investors rejected the acquisition immediately — preventing asset diversion on that occasion
Rapid withdrawal of proposal prevented immediate asset transfer
citation: Ramalinga Raju confessed 7 January 2009 — accounts had been falsified; inflated cash and bank balances, falsified profits; Wikipedia Satyam scandal; SCIRP academic fraud analysis; Dialnet academic case study; Government intervention, SEBI action, and board replacement followed
actual_outcome: Ramalinga Raju confessed on 7 January 2009 that Satyam's accounts had been falsified: cash and bank balances were inflated, profits were falsified over years. Government intervened, board was replaced. SEBI and CBI investigated. Tech Mahindra later acquired controlling stake. The case became known as 'India's Enron.'
documented_root_causes: Governance failure — board approved promoter self-dealing without scrutiny
Related-party transaction risk — attempted asset diversion to promoter entities
Financial-statement reliability risk — reported cash was not independently verified
Board oversight failure — independent directors did not exercise independence
Fraud risk — systematic falsification of accounts over years
Capital allocation red flag — promoter sought to use company cash for personal assets
Promoter-control risk — excessive promoter influence over board and management
final_business_state: Fraud confessed January 2009. Government intervention. Board replaced. SEBI and CBI investigation. Tech Mahindra acquired controlling stake. Company restructured and survived under new ownership.
